lessons.title: Poem 14: My Neighbour Friend Breathing His Last! (Bullah Shah; translated by A.R. Luther)
lessons.notes_html:
Exercise: Answer the following questions

1. When does a person remember God?

A person remembers God when he is faced with death and feels helpless. In the poem, when the poet sees his neighbour friend breathing his last, he cries out in shock, 'What should I do, O God! Aghast!' It is in the moment of death, when human power fails, that man turns to God.

2. What is the effect of the death scene?

The effect of the death scene is terror and shock. The poet is aghast: on every side there is talk of departing, and at every place there are shrieks in stock. Flames flare up in his heart to their height, and no charming sight remains visible to him. Everything charming in the world becomes invisible before the reality of death.

3. Why does a person feel helpless on the death of a friend?

A person feels helpless on the death of a friend because death cannot be stopped or delayed. The friend has to leave and cannot remain; his companions are already ready to catch the train — that is, the journey of death. Man can neither keep his friend back nor follow him, and so he stands aghast, crying, 'What should I do, O God!'

4. Without whose love is Bullah at a loss?

Without the love of God, Bullah is at a loss. The poet says, 'Without His love, Bullah in loss, / Can hardly dwell here or across.' That is, without God's love, man can hardly live in this world or in the next.

5. Write down the rhyming words used in the poem.

The rhyming words used in the poem are: last — Aghast; remain — train; talk — stock; height — sight; loss — across. The refrain 'What should I do, O God! Aghast!' closes every stanza.

6. The poet arrives at a certain conclusion in the last three lines of the poem. What is it? Write in your own words.

In the last three lines the poet arrives at the conclusion that the love of God is the only thing that matters. He says that without His love, Bullah is in loss and can hardly dwell here or across — that is, neither in this world nor in the next. All the charms of the world become invisible before death, and the only appreciable thing left is the love of God, without which everyone is at a loss.

7. Paraphrase the poem in your own words.

The poet says: My neighbour friend is breathing his last. What should I do, O God! I am terrified! He has to leave now and cannot remain; his companions are ready to catch the train of death. On every side there is talk of departing, and at every place there are shrieks and cries. Flames of grief flare up in my heart to their full height, and no charming sight is visible any more. Without the love of God, Bullah is in loss and can hardly live in this world or the next. What should I do, O God! I am terrified! The poem thus shows that death makes man helpless, and that only the love of God gives him support.

Key Points

  • A person remembers God when death comes near and human power fails.
  • The poet watches his neighbour friend breathing his last and cries, 'What should I do, O God! Aghast!'
  • Without the love of God, Bullah is at a loss — he can hardly dwell here or across.
  • Theme: only the love of God matters, in this world and the next.

lessons.title: Poem 15: He Came to Know Himself (Sachal Sarmast)
lessons.notes_html:
Exercise: Answer the following questions

1. Why does the poet put emphasis on how to know himself?

The poet puts emphasis on knowing oneself because one who knows himself also knows that he is a wonderful thing created by the Creator. Such a person cannot have a view of anything else except God Almighty. Self-knowledge is thus the door to God-knowledge: when man knows what he really is, he starts loving God, Who blesses him with great love, and every other thing becomes useless to him.

2. What makes one entangled in love?

The realization of God makes one entangled in love. When a person comes to know himself and realizes that he is created by God and that God is his Beloved, he gets enmeshed in love. The knowledge that God loves him, and that he exists only to know and love God, entangles him completely in divine love.

3. Why did Mansur mount the gallows?

Mansur mounted the gallows just to have his head cut off for the love of his Beloved, God. In the madness of divine love, he felt pleased and willing to be hanged on the gallows. Like Mansur, a person who is truly in love with God does not fear death; he gladly gives his head for his Beloved.

4. What is the bare Truth?

The bare Truth, which Sachu speaks plainly, is that God Himself came down to earth in love, and that man's stay in this world is only temporary. He who knows himself knows God, and knows that everything else is useless beside the love of the Beloved. The Truth is that union of one soul with another soul through the alchemy of love is the highest mystic truth.

5. Explain these lines: 'He alighted from high heaven / To pour a cascade of love'.

These lines mean that God came down from high heaven to earth out of love for mankind. Just as a cascade or waterfall pours down in abundance, God poured His love upon the world in full measure. The Divine descended from heaven so that man might know Him and love Him, and so that the dry hearts of men might be filled with the waters of divine love.

6. What does the poet say about 'His sojourn on earth' in the last line?

About 'His sojourn on earth' the poet says that it was temporary. A sojourn means a temporary stay in a place. God's stay on earth, like man's stay in this world, was not permanent: He came down in love, poured His cascade of love, and departed. The poet thus reminds us that this world is only a temporary abode, and that man should use his short stay here to know himself and to love God.

Key Points

  • To know oneself is to know God — one who knows himself knows he is a wonderful thing made by the Creator.
  • Mansur gladly mounted the gallows for the love of his Beloved.
  • God came down from high heaven to pour a cascade of love on earth — but His stay, like man's, was temporary.
  • Theme: self-knowledge is the door to God-knowledge.

lessons.title: Poem 16: God's Attributes (Jalaluddin Rumi; translated by Dr. Nicholson)
lessons.notes_html:
Exercises

1. How many attributes are mentioned in the poem?

Three attributes of God are mentioned in the poem: Seeing, Hearing and Knowing. God calls Himself 'Seeing', 'Hearing' and 'Knowing', each to a purpose for man's guidance.

2. What makes one scared of sinning?

The knowledge that God is All-Seeing makes one scared of sinning. God calls Himself 'Seeing' to the end that His eye may scare you from sinning: when a person remembers that God sees every deed, he becomes afraid to commit a sin.

3. What are the effects of the attributes of God?

The effects of the attributes of God are guidance and character-building. His attribute of Seeing restrains a person from doing wrong; His attribute of Hearing checks a person from using foul language; and His attribute of Knowing makes one afraid of plotting an evil against others. These names are not mere accidental titles; they are derived from God's attributes and have a real effect on man's conduct.

4. Mention three more attributes of God.

Three more attributes of God are: the Merciful (Al-Rahman), the Compassionate (Al-Rahim) and the Just (Al-Adl). Other attributes are the Creator, the Sustainer, the Forgiving and the All-Powerful.

5. How do these attributes help in refining the character of a person?

These attributes help in refining the character of a person by keeping him watchful over his deeds, words and thoughts. Remembering that God sees him stops him from sinning; remembering that God hears him stops him from foul talk; and remembering that God knows even his secret plans stops him from plotting evil. In this way the attributes of God become a constant guide, purifying a person's character day by day.

6. Do you think these attributes of God are remembered and kept in mind by us in our daily routine work?

No, I do not think that these attributes are properly remembered and kept in mind by us in our daily routine work. In the rush of daily life — in business, in studies and in conversation — most people forget that God sees, hears and knows everything. If we truly kept these attributes in mind, we would not cheat, abuse or plot against others. We should therefore make a habit of remembering them in every work we do, so that our daily life becomes honest and pure.

7. Make pairs of words similar in sound e.g. wait - weight. Words: end, scare, may, vain, lips, day, mere, talk, that, dare, bat, sheer, walk, crane, sips, bend.

The pairs of words similar in sound are: end — bend; scare — dare; may — day; lips — sips; mere — sheer; talk — walk; that — bat; vain — crane (slant rhyme).

Key Points

  • Three attributes of God are named: Seeing, Hearing and Knowing — each to guide man's conduct.
  • Seeing scares a person from sinning, Hearing checks foul language, Knowing stops secret plots of evil.
  • Remembering these attributes in daily life refines character and purifies conduct.
  • Theme: God's attributes are a constant guide for a good life.

lessons.title: Poem 17: The Delight Song (N. Scott Momaday)
lessons.notes_html:
Exercise: Answer the following questions

1. What do you understand when the poet says, 'I am the shadow that follows a child'?

When the poet says, 'I am the shadow that follows a child,' I understand that he feels playful, light and innocent, like a child's shadow. A child's shadow follows lightly and carelessly, without any burden or worry. The poet means that he too moves through life lightly and joyfully, in complete harmony with the world, like a happy child at play.

2. How can the crust of the snow glitter?

The crust of the snow can glitter when sunlight falls on its frozen surface. The hard, icy crust reflects the sun's rays in many directions, so that it shines and sparkles like a cluster of bright beads. That is why the poet calls himself 'the glitter on the crust of the snow' — he is part of that shining beauty of nature.

3. What is the dream of the poet?

The dream of the poet is the whole dream of all the beautiful things he names: to be a feather on the bright sky, a blue horse running in the plain, a fish rolling shining in the water, a shadow following a child, the evening light, an eagle playing with the wind, a cluster of bright beads, the farthest star, the cold of the dawn, the roaring of the rain, the glitter on the snow, the long track of the moon in a lake, and the flame of four colors. His dream is to be one with all these things — to live in complete harmony with nature.

4. What is the effect of man's good relation with the earth and the lords?

The effect of man's good relation with the earth and the lords is that he remains alive and active. The poet says, 'I stand in good relation to the earth, / I stand in good relation to the lords, / I stand in good relation to all that is beautiful, / I stand in good relation to all that is fruitful.' Because of these good relations, he is vivacious and full of life, and he can joyfully say, 'You see, I am alive, I am alive.'

5. What are the things that keep a person alive?

The things that keep a person alive are good relations: good relation with the earth, good relation with the lords, good relation with all that is beautiful, and good relation with all that is fruitful. Harmony with nature, with the atmosphere and with the universe keeps a person alive and active; it is this harmony, not wealth or power, that makes life delightful.

6. Pessimism and optimism are two attitudes of a human being. They describe the state of a person's mind who is hopeful at one moment and in despair at another. Can you tell which of these two attitudes goes well with this poem?

Optimism goes well with this poem. The poem is full of delight, life and hope: the poet feels light as a feather in the bright sky, finds no hurdles or difficulties anywhere in the universe, and is in complete harmony with everything. Again and again he declares, 'You see, I am alive, I am alive.' There is no despair in the poem at all; it is a song of joy, and therefore it expresses the optimistic attitude.

7. Write down your opinion in a few sentences based on the theme of the poem.

In my opinion, the theme of the poem is true and beautiful: a person is really alive only when he lives in good relation with the earth, with others and with all that is beautiful and fruitful. Delight does not come from wealth or power, but from harmony with nature — from feeling oneself a part of the sky, the wind, the rain, the snow and the moon. The poem teaches us to be optimistic, playful and light-hearted, like a feather or a child's shadow, and to find joy in the simple wonders around us.

Key Points

  • The poet is one with nature — a feather on the bright sky, a blue horse, a shadow following a child, the glitter on the snow.
  • He stands in good relation to the earth, to the lords, to all that is beautiful and all that is fruitful.
  • That harmony keeps him alive and full of delight — 'You see, I am alive, I am alive.'
  • Theme: optimism — delight comes from harmony with nature, not from wealth or power.

lessons.title: Poem 18: Love - an Essence of All Religions (Jalaluddin Rumi; translated by Dr. Nicholson)
lessons.notes_html:
Exercises

1. What is the effect of love?

The effect of love is that it changes all adversities into pleasures. Through love thorns become roses, vinegar becomes sweet wine, the stake becomes a throne, misfortune becomes good fortune, burning fire becomes pleasing light, stone becomes soft as butter, grief becomes a joy, lions become harmless, sickness becomes health, wrath seems to be a mercy, the dead rise to life, and the king becomes a slave. Love is the essence of all religions, and it transforms everything it touches.

2. Is life worth living without love?

No, life is not worth living without love. Life becomes a success and a pleasure only because of love; otherwise, as the Theme of the poem says, life is not worth living. Without love, thorns remain thorns, grief remains grief, and sickness remains sickness; it is love alone that turns them into roses, joy and health.

3. There are a number of antonyms in this poem. Write down the antonyms as given in the poem. Words: thorns, misfortune, stone, grief, sickness, wrath, dead, king.

The antonyms as given in the poem are: thorns — roses; misfortune — good fortune; stone — soft as butter (butter); grief — joy; sickness — health; wrath — mercy; dead — life; king — slave.

The pairs of rhyming words are: roses — poses; health — wealth; fight — light; joy — toy; thorn — horn; love — dove; gone — throne (slant rhyme).

Key Points

  • Love changes all adversities into pleasures: thorns become roses, grief becomes joy, sickness becomes health, the dead rise to life.
  • Love is the essence of all religions — without love, life is not worth living.
  • Antonyms in the poem: thorns — roses, misfortune — good fortune, stone — butter, grief — joy, sickness — health, wrath — mercy, dead — life, king — slave.

lessons.title: Poem 19: A Man of Words and Not of Deeds (Charles Perrault, 1628-1703; translated by Robert Samber)
lessons.notes_html:
Exercise: Answer the following questions

1. Paraphrase the poem.

A man who is all words and no deeds is like a garden full of weeds. When the weeds begin to grow, the garden becomes like a garden full of snow. When the snow begins to fall, it is like a bird sitting upon the wall. When the bird flies away, it is like an eagle in the sky. When the sky begins to roar, it is like a lion standing at the door. When the door begins to crack, it is like a stick struck across your back. When your back begins to smart with pain, it is like a penknife in your heart. And when your heart begins to bleed, you are dead and dead and dead indeed.

2. How does the life of man pass through different phases?

The life of man passes through different phases like the chain of images in the poem. It begins as a garden full of weeds — a life of useless talk. Then the weeds grow and the garden becomes cold and barren like snow in winter. Then comes a brief rest, like a bird upon the wall, followed by high flight like an eagle in the sky. Then danger comes, like a lion at the door, and punishment, like a stick across the back. Then pain, like a penknife in the heart, and finally the heart bleeds and life ends in death. Thus life passes from uselessness through danger and pain to its end.

3. What happens when life is spent with the help of words and not of deeds?

When life is spent with the help of words and not of deeds, it becomes useless like a garden full of weeds. The situation only grows worse, like snow in winter covering the garden, until pain and death follow. A man who only talks and boasts, and never does anything, wastes his life: his words lead to nothing, his condition aggravates step by step, and in the end he is dead and dead and dead indeed.

4. What does the garden look like when the weeds start growing?

When the weeds start growing, the garden looks like a garden full of snow. Just as snow covers a garden and makes it cold, white and barren, so the growing weeds cover the garden and choke all useful plants. The garden loses its beauty and fruitfulness and becomes a cold, useless waste.

5. Write down all the rhyming words in the poem and use them in sentences of your own.

The rhyming words in the poem, used in sentences, are: (1) deeds — weeds: A man of words and not of deeds is like a garden full of weeds. (2) grow — snow: When the weeds begin to grow, the garden is covered with snow. (3) fall — wall: When the snow begins to fall, the bird sits upon the wall. (4) fly — sky: When the bird away does fly, it looks like an eagle in the sky. (5) roar — door: When the sky begins to roar, it is like a lion at the door. (6) crack — back: When the door begins to crack, it feels like a stick across your back. (7) smart — heart: When your back begins to smart, it feels like a penknife in your heart. (8) bleed — indeed: When your heart begins to bleed, you are dead and dead and dead indeed.

6. What is the moral of the poem?

The moral of the poem is that a man must engage himself in some fruitful activity, and not merely in talk and boasting. Words without deeds are like weeds in a garden: they choke all that is useful, and they lead step by step to ruin and death. Only deeds make life pleasant and useful for humanity. A man should therefore do, and not merely say.

Key Points

  • A man of words and not of deeds is like a garden full of weeds — useless talk chokes all that is useful.
  • The poem builds a chain of ruin: weeds grow, snow falls, the bird flies, the sky roars, the lion waits, the stick strikes, the penknife pierces — and the heart bleeds.
  • Words without deeds lead step by step to ruin and death.
  • Moral: do, and do not merely say.

lessons.title: Poem 20: In Broken Images (Robert Graves)
lessons.notes_html:
Exercise: Answer the following questions

1. What is the state of two persons, one who trusts clear images and the other who mistrusts the broken images?

The person who trusts his clear images is quick but dull: he is quick in thinking because his images are clear, but he becomes dull because he trusts them without proof. He assumes their relevance and assumes the fact. The person who mistrusts his broken images is slow but sharp: he is slow because his images are broken, but he becomes sharp because he questions their relevance and questions the fact. Thus trust without inquiry makes a man dull, while doubt with inquiry makes him sharp.

2. Why does a person question his senses when the facts fail him?

A person questions his senses when the facts fail him because he had trusted his clear images completely and assumed the fact without questioning. When the fact fails, his whole trust collapses, and he has nothing left to blame except his own senses. He trusted his eyes and his mind blindly, so their failure leaves him doubting the very senses he relied upon.

3. Who is in a new confusion of his understanding?

'He' is in a new confusion of his understanding — the person who trusts his clear images. Because he never questioned anything, when the fact fails him he is left in a fresh confusion: his understanding itself becomes confused. By contrast, the speaker, who mistrusted his broken images all along, is in a new understanding of his confusion — he understands that he is confused, which is itself a kind of wisdom.

4. What is the moral lesson of the poem?

The moral lesson of the poem is that nothing should be taken for granted, and that a person should remain inquisitive about the images of life, whether they are broken or clear. One who trusts his clear images without proof becomes dull in life, whereas one who mistrusts his broken images becomes sharp and intelligent. Inquiry into the nature of things leads one to understand and accept the ground realities of life. Doubt, used honestly, is better than blind certainty.

5. Rewrite the poem in past tense.

He was quick, thinking in clear images; / I was slow, thinking in broken images. / He became dull, trusting to his clear images; / I became sharp, mistrusting my broken images. / Trusting his images, he assumed their relevance; / Mistrusting my images, I questioned their relevance. / Assuming their relevance, he assumed the fact; / Questioning their relevance, I questioned the fact. / When the fact failed him, he questioned his senses; / When the fact failed me, I approved my senses. / He continued quick and dull in his clear images; / I continued slow and sharp in my broken images. / He in a new confusion of his understanding; / I in a new understanding of my confusion.

6. Paraphrase the first four lines of the poem in your own words.

The first four lines say: He (the other person) is quick because he thinks in clear images, while I (the poet) am slow because I think in broken images. He becomes dull because he trusts his clear images blindly, while I become sharp because I mistrust my broken images. In other words, clear and easy thinking makes a man quick but dull, while difficult, doubtful thinking makes a man slow but sharp.

7. What conclusion does the poet draw in the last two lines of the poem? Write in detail.

In the last two lines the poet draws the conclusion: 'He in a new confusion of his understanding; / I in a new understanding of my confusion.' The man who trusted his clear images ends in a new confusion of his understanding: because he never questioned anything, the failure of the fact leaves his very understanding confused. The poet, who mistrusted his broken images and questioned everything, ends in a new understanding of his confusion: he knows that he is confused, and that knowledge is itself understanding. The conclusion is that honest doubt leads to true wisdom, while blind certainty leads only to deeper confusion.

Key Points

  • He who trusts his clear images is quick but dull; he who mistrusts his broken images is slow but sharp.
  • When the fact fails him, the man of clear images questions his senses and falls into a new confusion of his understanding.
  • The speaker, who questioned everything, reaches a new understanding of his confusion — and that is wisdom.
  • Moral: honest doubt is better than blind certainty; nothing should be taken for granted.

mcqs.why: The past-tense version in the notes says: 'When the fact failed him, he questioned his senses; when the fact failed me, I approved my senses.'

mcqs.q: What is the moral lesson of the poem?
options: Words without deeds lead to ruin
Nothing should be taken for granted; honest doubt is better than blind certainty
Delight comes from harmony with nature
Love is the essence of all religions
mcqs.why: The notes give the moral: nothing should be taken for granted, one should remain inquisitive, and doubt used honestly is better than blind certainty.
